Anthropic has announced the roll out of Personal Finance feature for its AI assistant Claude, enabling users to connect bank and card accounts and also ask questions about their finances in natural language. The company also said that the feature is created to help users get to better understand their spending, balances and transactions without switching between multiple banking apps. Claude Personal Finance feature: What it does. Users can ask questions such as where their money went this month, whether they are spending more than they earn, or what an APR is and how much interest they have been charged this year. Claude answers from the connected accounts’ balances and transactions, in everyday language, and explains unfamiliar terms. title: OCC: Banks need strong controls when delegating to AI agents
excerpt: Artificial Intelligence. OCC: Banks need strong controls when delegating to AI agents. By Ebrima Santos Sanneh. About Ebrima Santos. twitter. EbrimaSSanneh. mailto. ebrima. sanneh@arizent. com. linkedin. ebrima-santos-sanneh-2734b3146. Published November 05, 2026, 1:42 p. m. EST. |. Updated November 05, 2026, 2:21 p. m. EST. 4 Min Read. Facebook. Twitter. LinkedIn. Email. Key insight: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency says it does not treat AI as a standalone risk category, but rather discusses the liability banks' retain when they delegate authority to models which can make fraud, payment, or communicative decisions. Supporting data: The framework establishes six oversight pillars: purpose, potential risks, controls, human oversight, resilience and testing. The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency on Wednesday released guidance governing how examiners will grade banks on artificial intelligence deployment, concluding that banks need strong internal controls if they are going to delegate decision making to AI. Processing Content. The framework, while not binding, notes that the agency does not consider AI as a separate kind of regulatory risk, but rather directs examiners to apply existing regulatory criteria to the authority banks vest in AI systems, especially autonomous systems which may make decisions independent of human judgement. In those cases, OCC writes, a "bank's control intensity could increase. ". "Higher consequence use cases may warrant greater restrictions on autonomy, stronger controls, more direct human oversight, more independent validation, and more robust resilience measures," the guidance notes. "Risk classification may be based on potential consequences, transfer of agency, and the degree of human oversight, rather than the technical sophistication of the SI used. ". The guidance comes as banks are increasingly deploying AI to juice business productivity, but also are increasingly wary of the risks if AI makes mistakes. Federal Reserve Gov. Christopher Waller said in a recent speech that consumer trust is key to understanding who's on the hook when AI makes mistakes, like incorrectly purchasing an item. As some of the first federal banking guidance on AI, the OCC establishes six major "pillars" of supervisory guidance. Those include the purpose AI systems are directed to execute, the potential consequences if an AI system or agent fails its purpose, guardrails and human judgement, identifying who is accountable for AI oversight, a banks' ability to weather AI failures and evidence in the form of testing of AI systems and third-parties to ensure AI continues to be effective. Banks are given guidance on a variety of permissible use cases, including writing customer correspondence, credit decisions and autonomous use cases. The guidance repeatedly emphasizes the authority banks give AI models to execute independent actions. The OCC distinguishes between AI uses in which humans preapprove actions, vs when AI systems are monitored by humans, but may take action without preapproval. "The level of [human] involvement may be calibrated to the potential consequences, autonomy, reversibility and operating volume of the use case, among other factors," the agency writes. "Hallucinations concerning fees, rates, account status, or policies could contribute to legal or customer-harm exposure. "Banks may consider controls that limit automated representations, require verification in higher-impact contexts, and support prompt correction and remediation," the guidance continues. The agency says that AI overseers should have expertise and authority to intervene when necessary and that "where appropriate, the reviewer may be separate from the team that developed or owns the system. title: Deutsche Bank Private Bank launches AI Academy for more than 20,000 employees
excerpt: Themen: Education Education. Technology Technology. Media Release Frankfurt am Main, November 5, 2026. Deutsche Bank Private Bank launches AI Academy for more than 20,000 employees. Role-based AI learning tailored to employees’ responsibilities and level of AI experience. Training ranges from prompting and responsible AI use to advanced capabilities such as AI agents and Agentic AI. Already available to around 3,500 employees, with a global rollout planned for all Private Bank employees. Deutsche Bank’s Private Bank has launched the PB AI Academy, a new learning initiative designed to equip employees with the skills and confidence to use artificial intelligence effectively and responsibly in their day-to-day work. The PB AI Academy offers structured, role-based learning journeys tailored to employees’ responsibilities and level of AI experience. The Academy combines self-paced learning with instructor-led sessions, workshops and communities. Training ranges from foundational AI skills, including effective prompting and the responsible and ethical use of AI, to more advanced capabilities such as AI agents and Agentic AI. Each learning journey includes around five to ten recommended trainings, providing employees with a clear starting point from which to develop their AI capabilities. Yiping Li, Chief Operating Officer of the Private Bank of Deutsche Bank, said: “AI is making information more accessible than ever. What will increasingly set us apart is how we use it: applying judgement, expertise and a deep understanding of our clients. The PB AI Academy helps our people combine these strengths with the opportunities AI creates. ”. The PB AI Academy is already available to around 3,500 employees across the Private Bank’s international locations. Over the coming months, Deutsche Bank plans to expand the initiative to more than 20,000 Private Bank employees. In Germany, the Academy is expected to be introduced during the first half of 2027, following consultation with employee representatives. The Academy aims to strengthen AI literacy across the Private Bank, support the adoption of AI in day-to-day work and encourage experimentation, innovation and the sharing of best practices. title: Wealthsimple launches AI banking assistant that can help move money, place trades
excerpt: TORONTO — Wealthsimple is launching an AI assistant that can partially automate everyday banking activities and provide users with financial insights. The company announced a dozen new products at its Wealthsimple Presents event in Toronto on Thursday, including Penny, its new AI assistant. The company says Penny can cue up transactions like e-transfers, flag duplicate credit card charges, manage expenses and pay invoices, in addition to providing insights into users’ finances or giving advice on questions like how to maximize RRSP contributions. For self-directed investors, it can also help with buying or selling equities, ETFs or other assets. The company says the AI assistant won’t move money, place a trade or complete any other task without confirmation from the client. Latest updates on artificial intelligence news here. “So much of the friction that comes with a lot of these actions -- it’s getting them ready. If we’re talking about an e-transfer, it’s making sure I have the contact set up, I’m e-transferring the right amount. All of those things, the minutiae that block us on a day-to-day; the AI assistant can handle,” Jordan Deutsch, a director of software development at Wealthsimple, said in an interview. “When it comes time to actually hitting send, that’s an action that the user alone can take. ”. She added that the AI assistant exists within the Wealthsimple platform and doesn’t have access to the outside internet. “We don’t want to expose a whole wealth of outside data that we have less control over to our AI assistant,” she said. The launch comes as tech giants in Canada and the U. S. push toward integrating AI into commercial activities, leading to cybersecurity concerns. “What we’re not advocating is sharing your primary credentials with a third party … And at the same time, we know that a lot of clients want to use agents to engage with their finances. So, our objective is to create safe direct connections that don’t require credential sharing so that clients are empowered to do so,” Deutsch said. However, the company said that by early 2027, clients will be able to connect their Wealthsimple accounts to other AI tools like ChatGPT or Claude, based on the levels of access granted by the client. Some of the other products launched at the Wealthsimple Presents event include Wealthsimple Pay, which allows clients to send up to $100,000 instantly to other Wealthsimple clients, as well as temporary virtual cards that can offer more protection against fraud with custom expiry dates and spending limits. This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 5, 2026. Daniel Johnson, The Canadian Press.

title: OCC Releases Strict Supervisory Framework for Bank AI Use
excerpt: OCC Releases Strict Supervisory Framework for Bank AI Use. By PYMNTS | November 4, 2026. |. The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) has issued a supervisory framework designed to support the regulator’s examiners when they evaluate banks’ use of artificial intelligence and agentic AI in normal course business activities. The framework does not establish supervisory expectations for banks, does not set forth enforceable standards or prescriptive requirements, and is not meant to be used by banks to assess their use of Super Intelligence (SI) or their SI risk management, the OCC said in a Wednesday (Nov. 4) press release and summary of the “ OCC Supervisory Framework on Bank Use of Super Intelligence. ”. “ Super Intelligence ” is the term used by the executive branch in place of “artificial intelligence,” according to a Sept. 29 executive order signed by President Donald Trump. The OCC said in the release that it will adhere to a technology-neutral approach as it encourages safety, soundness and innovation and that it expects banks to conduct their activities in a safe and sound manner whether they’re using traditional methods or novel technologies. “Examiners may use the framework to identify SI-specific considerations that supplement existing model risk management, governance, technology, compliance and operational-risk practices and to tailor supervisory work to the nature and potential consequences of a bank’s SI use cases,” OCC said in the publication. “Examiners should not treat SI as a separate and distinct risk category, and banks are not required to define a separate SI risk appetite. ”. PYMNTS reported in May that the OCC highlighted AI as both a risk and an opportunity for innovation in its spring 2026 Semiannual Risk Perspective. In that publication, the OCC recommended that banks mitigate AI-enabled cyber risks by implementing more stringent security measures. The OCC also highlighted the opportunities for innovation with AI, noting that banks have used forms of artificial intelligence for years and are now exploring the use of generative AI and agentic AI. RSA Security CEO Greg Nelson said during a Monday (Nov. 2) interview with PYMNTS CEO Karen Webster that as bank employees deploy AI agents , the bank’s task is to keep track of the agents, identify those handling higher-risk work and confirm that the right human oversight is in place. “You [have to] know your agents, and you [have to] have the right discovery tool,” Nelson said. The PYMNTS Intelligence report “ Financial Services Pulls Ahead in the Enterprise AI Race ” found that financial services and insurance firms have reached high adoption of AI for 27 of the 75 tasks included in the survey. "For a lot of individuals who haven't really used it, it can feel a little intimidating. It feels like programming, it's doing all this technical stuff and individuals who are used to using Word or email can get a little intimidated and that can affect adoption. ". Getting staff onboard with AI is a challenge common to banks across the industry, according to Vikram Sivakumar, managing director and partner at Boston Consulting Group. "We are starting to recognize this as a change management issue, but one where the playbook is not necessarily fully available for everyone to play out with," Sivakumar said. When BCG surveys bank employees, the same three concerns always come up, he said: I'm afraid of losing my job, I don't trust AI and I don't have time to learn. "Solving that is both a conversation about how you create that structured approach and environment for a team to learn and behave in a new way, but also showing them that they have a job at the end of that transformation," Sivakumar said. "It isn't about taking their job away. ". Day of the Dead. And the bank runs a "Day of the Dead" to showcase failures within the organization – the ideas that were tried, that didn't work out and what can be learned from them. People who have tried something and been unsuccessful present their learnings to others in the company. "If you're not taking bold moves and not learning from those failures, you're not really moving forward," Mukhopadhyay said. The Bank of Cyprus has launched its first artificial intelligence-powered digital assistant, named "Danai" , as part of efforts to provide faster and more convenient customer service. Through the new assistant, customers can submit questions about banking products and services and receive answers without having to contact a member of staff for routine information. According to the bank, Danae can provide information about customer accounts and explain the various services offered by the bank. Among its practical functions is the ability to freeze a bank card , allowing customers to take immediate action through the digital service if necessary. The new platform uses artificial intelligence to communicate with users, following the model of digital assistants already deployed in other sectors, including the government's digital assistant. TAGS. #CY NEWS.

Export-Import Bank of Korea launches first EDCF AI project with $170m loan to Tanzania
excerpt: FINANCE Export-Import Bank of Korea launches first EDCF AI project with $170m loan to Tanzania. by Park Hye-rim Published : Nov. 5, 2026 - 09:37:53. Copy Completed!. View Korean Original. Institution to house 4 departments including AI and robotics. First use of 'K-AI Package' to link with data center, AI cluster. The Export-Import Bank of Korea is launching its first AI-sector project under the Economic Development Cooperation Fund, extending a $170 million loan to Tanzania to build an institution that will train specialists in AI, robotics and other advanced technologies. The bank announced Thursday that it had signed a $170 million EDCF loan agreement for Tanzania's "AI and Digital Technology Education Institution Construction Project. ". Senior Deputy Governor Lee Dong-hoon signed the agreement in Dar es Salaam on Wednesday with Natu Mwamba, Tanzania's deputy finance minister. The EDCF is a long-term, low-interest loan fund that supports the construction of economic and social infrastructure in developing countries; the Export-Import Bank of Korea administers it under a mandate from the Ministry of Economy and Finance. The project marks the first time the EDCF has channeled funds into the AI sector. It is also the inaugural project under the government's "K-AI Package," an initiative that uses concessional loans to help developing countries build infrastructure and adopt AI technology simultaneously. The project site covers 35,000 square meters. A technical education institution will be built there to train personnel in physical AI — a field combining AI with robots and other machines that enables systems to perceive, reason and act in real-world environments. The institution will house four departments: AI, robotics, data analytics and the Internet of Things. It will also include a high-performance AI training facility equipped with AI laboratories, AI computing units, high-speed memory chips and fast networking infrastructure. South Korean AI technology and educational systems will be used in both instruction and institutional operations. The facility will adopt an online system for managing learning and assessment, as well as a cloud system for sharing curricula in real time. The Tanzanian government plans to develop a large-scale AI data center and AI cluster near the institution and attract related companies to the area. The Export-Import Bank of Korea intends to use the project as a springboard for South Korean AI and digital companies to enter Africa's infrastructure market. "We will use this EDCF support to Tanzania, which is strategically nurturing its AI and digital industries, to solidify the foundation for expanding our presence in Africa," Lee said. "We will make this project the first step toward planting Korean AI technology on the continent, and actively back Korean companies' entry into overseas infrastructure projects across EDCF priority areas — including AI and digital, culture, and supply chains. ". Meanwhile, the bank signed a memorandum of understanding on nuclear power project financing cooperation with Turkey's nuclear energy authority on Wednesday, agreeing to help structure financing for the new Sinop nuclear power plant project. The Export-Import Bank of Korea plans to review financing options from the project's earliest stages to support Team Korea's bid to win the contract. rim@heraldcorp. com. excerpt: A new initiative will bring together firms, quantum technology providers, and national research labs to explore practical applications of quantum computing. The FCA will bring together financial services firms, quantum technology providers and national research laboratories to explore how quantum computing could help tackle financial crime. The Quantum Experimentation Group , the first of its kind for a regulator, will initially explore how quantum machine learning could help detect money laundering and fraud. It will launch in the first quarter of 2027. Participants will use an FCA synthetic dataset – artificially generated data – to help overcome a key barrier to testing: access to suitable data. The group will help firms explore practical uses of quantum computing in financial services and share findings to guide future testing. It will also help the FCA understand the technology’s opportunities and limitations, barriers to experimentation and what these could mean for regulation. Jessica Rusu, chief data, information and intelligence officer at the FCA, said: 'We want to help firms explore where quantum could make a meaningful difference, and early experimentation is essential to understanding its potential in financial services. By bringing together firms, technology providers and researchers we can build readiness and identify practical applications for common industry challenges, starting with financial crime. '. The initiative builds on the FCA’s research into the long-term potential of quantum computing in financial services. Financial services firms, quantum technology providers and national research laboratories can register their interest in joining the group by 31 December 2026. Notes to editors. Read more about the Quantum Experimentation Group and how to register an interest in joining the group. The FCA’s Quantum Experimentation Group will be the world’s first regulator-led quantum computing experimentation group. The group will support organisations at different stages of their quantum journey, from those beginning to explore potential use cases to those already undertaking advanced experimentation. As part of the initiative, the FCA will define problem statements and work alongside participants to build understanding of the opportunities, limitations and practical considerations associated with quantum technologies. The initiative will complement wider activity across the UK’s quantum ecosystem by creating additional opportunities for collaborative experimentation and learning.
